summary.text: Multiplying the sum by \(2n\) yields \(H_n=F_{2n+1}+F_{2n-1}-1\), so integrality is equivalent to \(2n\mid H_n\); the recurrence \(H_{n+2}+H_n=3H_{n+1}+1\) gives immediate mod-\(4\) contradictions when \(3\mid n\) or \(n\) is even. For the remaining odd case, Cassini gives \(H_n=(F_{n+1}+F_{n-1})^2+1\); taking the least prime factor of \(n\), quadratic-nonresidue and periodic computations modulo \(5,13,17\) handle the exceptional cases, while a Fibonacci rank-of-apparition argument for larger primes produces a smaller prime factor of \(n\), contradicting minimality.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1i\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1}.
\]
We prove that, for every integer \(n>1\), this rational number is not an integer. This is equivalent to saying that its denominator in lowest terms is not \(1\).

Throughout, let \(F_0=0,F_1=1\), and \(F_{r+2}=F_{r+1}+F_r\) be the Fibonacci sequence. Define the integer
\[
 H_n=\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\binom{2n-i}{i}+\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1}\right).
\]

We first reduce the problem to a divisibility assertion about \(H_n\).

For \(1\leq i\leq n\), the standard adjacent-binomial identity gives
\[
 i\binom{2n-i}{i}=(2n-i)\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 i\left(\binom{2n-i}{i}+\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1}\right)
 &=((2n-i)+i)\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1}\\
 &=2n\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Dividing by \(i\) and summing from \(1\) to \(n\), we obtain
\[
 2nS_n=H_n. \tag{1}
\]
Thus
\[
 S_n=\frac{H_n}{2n}.
\]
Since \(H_n\) and \(2n\) are integers and \(2n>0\), the reduced denominator of \(S_n\) is \(1\) if and only if
\[
 2n\mid H_n. \tag{2}
\]
It remains to prove that (2) is impossible when \(n>1\).

We next put \(H_n\) into Fibonacci form. We use the familiar identity
\[
 F_{N+1}=\sum_{j\geq0}\binom{N-j}{j}, \tag{3}
\]
where terms with \(j>N-j\) vanish. Identity (3) follows immediately by induction from Pascal's identity: the right side for \(N\) is the sum of the corresponding expressions for \(N-1\) and \(N-2\), and its initial values are \(1,1\).

Taking \(N=2n\) in (3) gives
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{2n-i}{i}=F_{2n+1}.
\]
The term with \(i=0\) is \(1\), so
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^{n}\binom{2n-i}{i}=F_{2n+1}-1.
\]
In the second sum defining \(H_n\), put \(j=i-1\). Then (3), with \(N=2n-2\), gives
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^{n}\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1}
 =\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{2n-2-j}{j}=F_{2n-1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 H_n=F_{2n+1}+F_{2n-1}-1. \tag{4}
\]

The elementary Fibonacci identity
\[
 F_{r+4}+F_r=3F_{r+2}
\]
follows by expanding both sides with the Fibonacci recurrence. Applying it at the two indices \(2n+1\) and \(2n-1\), and using (4), yields, for every \(n\geq1\),
\[
 H_{n+2}+H_n=3H_{n+1}+1. \tag{5}
\]
Also, directly from the definition or (4),
\[
 H_1=2,\qquad H_2=6. \tag{6}
\]
We shall repeatedly use (5) for modular computations.

We first dispose of two broad classes of \(n\). From (5) and (6), induction gives
\[
 H_n\equiv
 \begin{cases}
 1\pmod4,&3\mid n,\\
 2\pmod4,&3\nmid n.
 \end{cases} \tag{7}
\]
For completeness, this induction has period three. Starting from the pair \((H_1,H_2)\equiv(2,2)\pmod4\), the rule
\(H_{r+2}\equiv3H_{r+1}+1-H_r\pmod4\) produces
\[
 2,2,1,2,2,1,\ldots,
\]
which is exactly (7).

If \(3\mid n\), (7) says that \(H_n\) is odd, whereas \(2n\) is even. Hence \(2n\nmid H_n\).

If \(3\nmid n\) and \(n\) is even, then \(4\mid2n\), while (7) says \(H_n\equiv2\pmod4\). Again \(2n\nmid H_n\).

It remains only to treat the case
\[
 n>1,\qquad n\text{ odd},\qquad 3\nmid n. \tag{8}
\]
Assume, for a contradiction, that
\[
 2n\mid H_n. \tag{9}
\]

We collect several identities and congruence facts needed for this last case.

First, Cassini's identity in the form
\[
 F_{k+1}^2-F_{k+2}F_k=(-1)^k \tag{10}
\]
follows by induction from the Fibonacci recurrence. The standard doubling identity
\[
 F_{2r+1}=F_{r+1}^2+F_r^2 \tag{11}
\]
then gives, when \(n\) is odd,
\[
 F_{2n+1}+F_{2n-1}
   =(F_{n+1}+F_{n-1})^2+2. \tag{12}
\]
Indeed, applying (11) at \(n\) and at \(n-1\), the left side is
\[
 F_{n+1}^2+2F_n^2+F_{n-1}^2.
\]
Because \(n-1\) is even, Cassini gives
\[
 F_n^2=F_{n+1}F_{n-1}+1,
\]
and substitution turns the preceding expression into
\((F_{n+1}+F_{n-1})^2+2\). Combining (12) with (4), we have
\[
 H_n=(F_{n+1}+F_{n-1})^2+1 \qquad(n\text{ odd}). \tag{13}
\]

It follows at once that if a prime \(p\equiv3\pmod4\) divides both \(n\) and \(H_n\), then a contradiction results: modulo \(p\), equation (13) would say that \(-1\) is a square. But for a prime \(p\equiv3\pmod4\), \(-1\) is not a quadratic residue. Explicitly, if \(x^2=-1\), then Fermat's theorem gives \(x^{p-1}=1\), whereas
\[
 x^{p-1}=(x^2)^{(p-1)/2}=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}=-1.
\]
Thus, under (9), no prime divisor of \(n\) can be congruent to \(3\pmod4\).

We also need three small modular exclusions. Iterating (5) modulo \(5\) gives
\[
 H_{2k+1}\equiv2\pmod5,\qquad H_{2k+2}\equiv1\pmod5. \tag{14}
\]
The initial pair is \((2,1)\pmod5\), and one application of (5) to each member returns the same pair. Since \(n\) is odd, (14) says \(H_n\equiv2\pmod5\). Therefore \(5\mid n\) is incompatible with (9).

Similarly, recurrence (5) gives the following complete period modulo \(13\): for \(r=1,\ldots,14\),
\[
 (H_r\bmod13)=(2,6,4,7,5,9,10,9,5,7,4,6,2,1), \tag{15}
\]
and this block repeats with period \(14\). To check this, begin with \(2,6\), repeatedly replace consecutive residues \(a,b\) by \(b,3b+1-a\), and reduce modulo \(13\). The last two residues are \(2,1\), and the next two are again \(2,6\), so induction proves the repetition. None of the entries in (15) is zero. Hence
\[
 13\nmid H_m\quad\text{for every }m\geq1. \tag{16}
\]
In particular, \(13\mid n\) is incompatible with (9).

Modulo \(17\), the analogous block of length \(18\) is
\[
 (H_r\bmod17)=
 (2,6,0,12,3,15,9,13,14,13,9,15,3,12,0,6,2,1) \tag{17}
\]
for \(r=1,\ldots,18\), and this block repeats. Again, every entry follows successively from \(c\equiv3b+1-a\pmod{17}\); the end of the block restarts the initial pair. The only zero entries occur for indices congruent to \(3\) or \(15\pmod{18}\), and both kinds of indices are divisible by \(3\). Consequently,
\[
 3\nmid m\implies17\nmid H_m. \tag{18}
\]
By (8), \(17\mid n\) is therefore also incompatible with (9).

We now establish the descent argument that excludes all remaining, larger prime factors. We need two further Fibonacci identities. For odd \(n\),
\[
 (F_{2n+1}+F_{2n-1})^2=5F_{2n}^2+4. \tag{19}
\]
One way to derive this is to write \(n=2k+1\), apply Cassini at the odd index \(2k+1\), and use
\(F_{2k+3}=F_{2k+2}+F_{2k+1}\); expansion gives
\((F_{2k+3}+F_{2k+1})^2=5F_{2k+2}^2+4\), and replacing \(k\) appropriately yields (19). Since (4) says
\(F_{2n+1}+F_{2n-1}=H_n+1\), equation (19) becomes
\[
 (H_n+1)^2=5F_{2n}^2+4,
\]
or equivalently
\[
 H_n(H_n+2)=5F_{2n}^2+3. \tag{20}
\]
The second identity is
\[
 F_{6n}=F_{2n}\bigl(5F_{2n}^2+3\bigr). \tag{21}
\]
For example, this follows from the Fibonacci addition formula
\[
 F_{u+v+1}=F_uF_v+F_{u+1}F_{v+1},
\]
together with the doubling formulas and Cassini; after expressing \(F_{4n-1}\) and \(F_{4n}\) in terms of \(F_{2n-1},F_{2n},F_{2n+1}\), expansion and Cassini reduce the result to (21). Equivalently, (21) is the usual triple-angle identity \(F_{3m}=F_m(5F_m^2+3(-1)^m)\) with \(m=2n\).

Now let \(p\) be any prime such that \(p\mid H_n\). By (20),
\[
 p\mid 5F_{2n}^2+3,
\]
and (21) therefore implies
\[
 p\mid F_{6n}. \tag{22}
\]

We shall use the rank of apparition of \(p\) in the Fibonacci sequence. Let \(a\) be the least positive integer such that
\[
 p\mid F_a.
\]
Such an \(a\) exists here by (22). The strong divisibility property
\[
 \gcd(F_r,F_s)=F_{\gcd(r,s)} \tag{23}
\]
implies
\[
 p\mid F_m\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\mid m. \tag{24}
\]
Indeed, if \(p\mid F_m\), then (23) shows that \(p\mid F_{\gcd(a,m)}\). Minimality of \(a\), together with \(0<\gcd(a,m)\leq a\), forces \(\gcd(a,m)=a\), so \(a\mid m\). Conversely, if \(a\mid m\), the standard divisibility property \(F_a\mid F_m\) gives \(p\mid F_m\).

We also require a bound on \(a\).

**Entry-point bound.** If \(p\geq13\) is prime, then
\[
 p\mid F_{p-1}\quad\text{or}\quad p\mid F_{p+1}. \tag{25}
\]
In particular, the least positive \(a\) with \(p\mid F_a\) satisfies
\[
 a<3p. \tag{26}
\]

Here is a proof of (25). Work over \(\mathbb F_p\) in the two-dimensional commutative algebra
\[
 R=\mathbb F_p[\omega]/(\omega^2-5).
\]
Thus elements are pairs \(x+y\omega\), with multiplication determined by \(\omega^2=5\). Since \(p\neq2,5\), define
\[
 \phi=\frac{1+\omega}{2},\qquad \psi=\frac{1-\omega}{2}.
\]
Then
\[
 \phi+\psi=1,\qquad \phi\psi=-1,
 \qquad \phi^2=\phi+1,
 \qquad \psi^2=\psi+1. \tag{27}
\]
Induction using the last two identities gives the Binet relation in \(R\):
\[
 \phi^m-\psi^m=\omega F_m. \tag{28}
\]
Looking at the coefficient of \(\omega\), (28) shows
\[
 p\mid F_m\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \phi^m=\psi^m. \tag{29}
\]

Set \(c=5^{(p-1)/2}\in\mathbb F_p\). Fermat's theorem gives \(c^2=5^{p-1}=1\), so, because \(\mathbb F_p\) is a field,
\[
 c=1\quad\text{or}\quad c=-1. \tag{30}
\]
The Frobenius map in the characteristic-\(p\) algebra \(R\) satisfies \((x+y)^p=x^p+y^p\). Also
\[
 \omega^p=\omega^{p-1}\omega=(\omega^2)^{(p-1)/2}\omega=c\omega.
\]
It follows that if \(c=1\), then \(\phi^p=\phi\) and \(\psi^p=\psi\); while if \(c=-1\), then \(\phi^p=\psi\) and \(\psi^p=\phi\).

In the first case, \(\phi\) and \(\psi\) are units because \(\phi\psi=-1\), so
\(\phi^{p-1}=\psi^{p-1}=1\). By (29), \(p\mid F_{p-1}\). In the second case,
\[
 \phi^{p+1}=\psi\phi=-1=\phi\psi=\psi^{p+1},
\]
so (29) gives \(p\mid F_{p+1}\). This proves (25), and (26) follows by minimality since both \(p-1\) and \(p+1\) are positive and less than \(3p\).

We can now perform the descent. Suppose \(p\geq29\) is a prime divisor of \(n\). By (9), \(p\mid H_n\), so (22) applies. Let \(a\) be the least positive index for which \(p\mid F_a\). From (22) and (24),
\[
 a\mid6n. \tag{31}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
 a\nmid2n. \tag{32}
\]
For if \(a\mid2n\), (24) gives \(p\mid F_{2n}\). We already have \(p\mid H_n\); reducing (20) modulo \(p\) would then give \(p\mid3\), impossible for \(p\geq29\).

Equations (31) and (32) force \(3\mid a\). Indeed, if \(a\) were coprime to \(3\), then from \(a\mid(2n)\cdot3\), Euclid's lemma would give \(a\mid2n\), contrary to (32). Write
\[
 b=\frac a3.
\]
Cancelling the factor \(3\) in \(a=3b\mid3(2n)\) gives
\[
 b\mid2n. \tag{33}
\]
Moreover, by the entry-point bound,
\[
 a<3p,
\]
so
\[
 b<p. \tag{34}
\]

Remove from \(b\) its possible factor \(2\) by setting
\[
 d=\frac{b}{\gcd(b,2)}.
\]
Because \(\gcd(b,2)\) is either \(1\) or \(2\), (33) implies
\[
 d\mid n. \tag{35}
\]
Also \(d\leq b<p\).

We claim \(d\geq2\). If \(d=1\), then either \(\gcd(b,2)=1\), in which case \(b=1\) and \(a=3\), or \(\gcd(b,2)=2\), in which case \(b=2\) and \(a=6\). But \(p\mid F_a\), whereas
\[
 F_3=2,\qquad F_6=8,
\]
which is impossible for \(p\geq29\). Thus \(d>1\).

Choose a prime divisor \(q\) of \(d\). From (35),
\[
 q\mid n,
\]
and from \(q\leq d<p\),
\[
 q<p. \tag{36}
\]
We have proved the crucial descent statement: every prime divisor \(p\geq29\) of \(n\), under assumptions (8) and (9), forces a strictly smaller prime divisor \(q\) of \(n\).

We now finish the proof by applying this to the least prime divisor \(p\) of \(n\). Since \(n>1\), such a prime exists. Because \(n\) is odd, \(p\neq2\), and because \(3\nmid n\), \(p\neq3\). Every remaining prime falls into one of the following classes:

1. \(p=5\);
2. \(p\equiv3\pmod4\);
3. \(p=13\);
4. \(p=17\);
5. \(p\geq29\).

To see that this list is exhaustive, an odd prime other than \(3\) is congruent to \(1\) or \(3\pmod4\). In the \(1\pmod4\) class, the values below \(29\) are \(5,9,13,17,21,25\); among these, only \(5,13,17\) are prime.

Each class is impossible. If \(p=5\), then \(5\mid n\), contradicting (14) and (9). If \(p\equiv3\pmod4\), equation (13) makes \(-1\) a square modulo \(p\), which is impossible. If \(p=13\), then (9) gives \(13\mid H_n\), contradicting (16). If \(p=17\), then (9) gives \(17\mid H_n\), contradicting (18), since \(3\nmid n\). Finally, if \(p\geq29\), the descent produces a prime \(q\mid n\) with \(q<p\), contradicting the choice of \(p\) as the least prime divisor of \(n\).

Thus (9) is impossible in the remaining odd case as well. Combining this with the two earlier cases, we have shown that
\[
 2n\nmid H_n
\]
for every \(n>1\). By (1) and (2), \(S_n=H_n/(2n)\) is therefore never an integer for \(n>1\). Hence the denominator of
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^n\frac1i\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1}
\]
in lowest terms is not \(1\), as claimed.
